project.name: Holiday flash sale
project.summary: A one-page web shop for a midnight sneaker drop: 100 pairs of limited-edition sneakers at $49.99, one pair per customer. Shoppers sign in with their email address, enter a shipping address and press Buy now; the server charges the card through a payment provider and confirms the order. About 3,000 visitors are expected in the first minute after an email announcement. Status: built and piloted with staff on 16 October 2026; not live. No review pack was handed in: the author's sections of this pack were filled in by the reviewer from the repository and are marked as such.

verdict.reason: The shop cannot be delivered as it is. Under the expected midnight rush it sells far more pairs than it has and charges people twice, anyone can read customers' addresses or wipe all orders, one bad request or a restart takes the sale down and loses paid orders, and it is not connected to a real payment provider.

blockers.text: Make the purchase safe: the price comes from the server, stock is reserved atomically before charging, one pair per customer is enforced in the database, every purchase carries one idempotency key, a time-out leaves the order pending, and a job settles and reconciles payments.
blockers.why: Today a rush oversells and double-charges, and money can move with no order.

blockers.text: Close access: a real sign-in with signed sessions, an ownership check on every order, admin routes removed or behind an admin role, and the search route fixed or removed.
blockers.why: Anyone can read or change other customers' data and wipe the sale.

blockers.text: Rotate the payment key that is written in the code, move it to a secret setting and remove it from the history.
blockers.who: Developer, with whoever owns the payment provider account
blockers.why: Anyone with a copy of the code holds the key.

blockers.text: Keep orders safe across crashes and deploys: a persistent database with backups and migrations, no deletion at start-up, error handling that answers 400 instead of crashing, and a graceful shutdown.
blockers.why: One bad request or a restart takes the site down and erases every order.

blockers.text: Connect the real payment provider and try a purchase, a decline and a refund in its test mode, then one small live purchase and refund.

blockers.text: Make the page hold the expected crowd and keep bots out: one query per page view with a short cache, a waiting room or busy page, and limits on sign-ins and purchases; then pass the load and race tests on a staging copy.
blockers.why: The page slows to 2 to 8 seconds from half the expected crowd, and scripts can buy without limit.

blockers.text: Prepare to run the sale: health checks, error tracking and alerts to a named person, clean logs, backups and a rollback that have been tried, and a rehearsed launch runbook.

verdict.ifLaunchedNow: Within the first minute, hundreds of customers would be charged for sneakers that do not exist and many would be charged twice, while the page took several seconds to load. Anyone could download every buyer's email and home address, buy at a price they choose, or delete all orders with one request; a single malformed request would stop the sale for everyone, and the restart would erase every paid order. The client would face refunds, chargebacks, a personal-data breach to report, and angry customers on launch night.

architecture.summary: One Node.js process serves the page and a small JSON API from an in-memory SQLite database (wrapped to behave like a hosted database with a pool of 10 connections). A purchase reads the stock, charges the card through the payment provider, writes the stock and the order, and sends an email, all inside the request. The payment provider and email are simulators. (Reviewer-built: the author handed in no architecture; full map in `01-system-map.md`.)

race.summary: 1,000 buyers each clicked Buy twice at the same moment for 100 pairs. Every click was either accepted or failed; none was refused as sold out or already ordered.

performance.slowPartner: With the provider taking 3 to 10 seconds per charge, 200 buyers clicking twice produced 400 charges and 400 orders for 100 pairs, and the stock counter ended at 99. classes.name: Customers charged twice for one purchase

occurrences.text: Charged twice for one pair (closed: "could not reproduce by clicking once")
Double charge again: clicked once, then reloaded while the page was loading

classes.rootCause: A purchase has no identity: each request is a new purchase, with no idempotency key sent to the provider and no rule that a customer has one order per product. The ticket was closed because a single click could not reproduce it, and nobody tested a double click or a reload during payment.
classes.control: A unique rule on (customer, product) in the database, an idempotency key per purchase attempt passed to the provider, and the double-click acceptance test (AC-04) plus the race test with two clicks per buyer, run on every change.
classes.controlCheck: Run against this commit: AC-04 fails in all three runs (2 orders after a double-click) and the race test reports 957 buyers charged twice, so both tests catch it. Neither runs automatically yet.
classes.agentRule: Every purchase carries one idempotency key from the page to the provider; never create an order without it. AC-04 and the race test must pass.

classes.name: More sold than in stock, and more than one pair per customer

occurrences.text: One person bought 3 pairs although the limit is one per customer
Pilot stock was 20 pairs; 37 paid orders

classes.rootCause: The business rules live only as an if-statement in application code, followed by a separate write of a number read earlier; the database has no constraint, and the card is charged between the check and the write, which widens the gap. Nobody tested many buyers at once.
classes.control: An atomic reservation (`UPDATE … SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0`), `CHECK (stock >= 0)` and a unique (customer, product) rule in the database, proven by the race test in CI.
classes.controlCheck: The race test on this commit: 1,957 orders for 100 pairs (it catches it). The Semgrep rule `stock-lost-update-sql` also fired on `app/server.mjs:111`.
classes.agentRule: Stock and per-customer limits are enforced only by the database (atomic update, constraints); never check-then-write in code. The race test must pass.

classes.name: Customers charged but no order recorded

occurrences.text: After a restart, two testers who had paid had no order
Card charged, the page said sold out, and no order

classes.rootCause: The purchase charges the card before it records anything, keeps orders only in memory and deletes them at start-up, and has no "pending" state or reconciliation with the provider. Any interruption between charge and record (crash, deploy, error) loses the order while the money is taken.
classes.control: A pending order written before the charge, a durable database with no destructive start-up, a settlement and reconciliation job that alerts on any difference, and an integration test that interrupts a purchase and restarts the app.
classes.controlCheck: No control exists. The reviewer's reproduction (`evidence/probes-charged-no-order.txt`) shows the gap and can become that test.
classes.agentRule: Never charge before a pending order is stored; never delete data at start-up; every provider charge must have an order (reconciliation must report zero differences).

classes.name: The server trusts the browser: someone else's data, the price, admin functions

occurrences.text: Changing the number in an order link showed another customer's name and address
Anyone can open the sales stats page

classes.rootCause: There is no server-side authority: identity is an unsigned token the browser can write, the price is whatever the browser sends, and each route decides for itself whether to check anything, so some check nothing at all.
classes.control: Signed sessions verified in one place for every route, a deny-by-default rule for admin routes, prices read from the database, and tests that call every route as nobody, as another customer and with a tampered price; the Semgrep rules `unverified-token-decode`, `price-from-client` and `admin-route-inventory` in CI.
classes.controlCheck: AC-03 and AC-06 fail on this commit (they catch the price and privacy problems); the three Semgrep rules fired on lines 46, 105, 132 and 139. No test calls the admin routes without credentials.
classes.agentRule: Every route checks a signed session on the server; prices and permissions come from the database, never from the request. AC-03, AC-06 and the admin-access test must pass.

areaNotes.S: Access control is missing almost everywhere: anyone can act as any customer, read any order, use the admin functions and dump the order table through the search route. A key named like a live payment key is in the code. These need fixing before anything else.
areaNotes.A: The design keeps everything in one process's memory and does the whole purchase (check, charge, write, email) inside one request, with the card charged first. That is why it oversells, double-charges and loses paid orders on any restart.
areaNotes.D: None of the seven business rules is enforced where it cannot be bypassed; every one of them was broken with a direct request or a race test.
areaNotes.P: The sale page manages about half the expected opening crowd, and the rush breaks the stock and one-per-customer rules. Page speed for a single phone visitor is good.
areaNotes.O: Nothing is in place to notice, survive or recover from problems on the night: no monitoring, health checks, backups, rollback, runbook or graceful restart.
areaNotes.H: The acceptance suite is a good start: one test per criterion, outcomes checked, three runs without retries. But it fails on the delivered commit, nothing runs it automatically, and it misses crashes, restarts, admin access and what should disappear from the screen.
areaNotes.Q: Every one of the 16 pilot tickets traces to a design gap, not bad luck. Three tickets were closed without a fix, and each problem came back.
areaNotes.R: The app starts from the README in a minute, but there is no review pack, no staging copy, no agreed recovery targets, and the settings described in the README do not match the code.
areaNotes.U: The agreed criteria are good and numbered; six of the Must criteria fail in every run and the never-oversell criterion fails the race test.

findings.title: Anyone can read any customer's order, including their home address
findings.where: `app/server.mjs:120-124` (`GET /api/orders/:id`): no sign-in or ownership check. **Evidence:** With no token, `curl -s localhost:3310/api/orders/1` returned Alice's email, address and amount with HTTP 200 (`evidence/probes-access.txt`, step 1). Acceptance test AC-06 failed in all three runs: Bob and a logged-out visitor both got HTTP 200. **Tickets:** #8.
findings.impact: Anyone can collect every buyer's email address and home address by trying order numbers 1, 2, 3 and so on.
findings.evidence: With no token, `curl -s localhost:3310/api/orders/1` returned Alice's email, address and amount with HTTP 200 (`evidence/probes-access.txt`, step 1). Acceptance test AC-06 failed in all three runs: Bob and a logged-out visitor both got HTTP 200.
findings.fix: Require a signed-in customer and look the order up by id and customer together (`WHERE id = ? AND customer = ?`); answer 404 otherwise.
findings.doneWhen: AC-06 passes three runs in a row, and the request in `evidence/probes-access.txt` step 1 answers 401 or 404.

findings.title: Anyone can act as any customer: the sign-in "token" is just the email address, unsigned
findings.where: `app/server.mjs:79-83` (`POST /api/login` returns base64 of whatever email it is given) and `app/server.mjs:42-47` (`currentUser` decodes the token without checking a signature); `TOKEN_SECRET` (`run.mjs:21`) is never read. **Evidence:** A token made by hand (`printf '{"email":"alice@example.test"}' | base64`), without signing in, returned Alice's orders from `GET /api/my-orders` (`evidence/probes-access.txt`, step 2).
